<think>We need to answer: Explain CAP theorem, give for each combination (CA, CP, AP) three real-world systems. Also give mathematical formal definition.

We must ensure compliance with policy: no disallowed content. This is fine.

We should include a formal definition: CAP theorem states that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously provide more than two of the three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance. Usually partition tolerance is required, so we choose between C and A. But we can also discuss CA (not partition tolerant), CP (consistency and partition tolerance), AP (availability and partition tolerance). Provide examples: CA: traditional RDBMS with single-node or cluster without partitions; CP: HBase, Zookeeper, MongoDB with majority config; AP: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB.

We need to give three real-world systems for each combination. Provide details about why they belong to each category.

Also include mathematical formal definition: using state machine, safety and liveness properties, etc. Provide definitions of consistency (linearizability), availability (every request receives a response), partition tolerance (network partition may happen). Formal: a system can be modeled as a distributed automaton; the theorem states that any such system cannot satisfy all three properties in the presence of network partitions.

We can also discuss the "2 out of 3" concept and nuance: partitions are rare but must be considered. Provide examples of systems that can be configured to be CP or AP.

We can also mention that CAP is about trade-offs, not a binary classification; many systems can be tuned.

We need to include three real-world systems per combination: CA: MySQL (single-master replication, no partition tolerance), PostgreSQL (synchronous replication in a single data center), etc. CP: etcd, Consul, Zookeeper, MongoDB (with appropriate config), HBase, etc. AP: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, Amazon S3 (eventual consistency), etc.

We need to provide details for each.

We can also mention that CA is essentially not a realistic scenario for distributed systems across wide area networks, but can be used within a single data center.

We can also include a short note about the "PACELC" model for further nuance.

We can also discuss formal definitions: a system is a set of nodes, each with state, and a set of operations; a network partition is a subset of nodes that cannot communicate with another subset; a system is consistent if all nodes see the same sequence of operations (or linearizable); a system is available if every request eventually receives a response; a system tolerates partitions if the system continues to operate correctly despite partitions.

Define "correctness" under the CAP theorem: a system is correct if it is consistent and available for all possible executions, including those with partitions.

The theorem: there is no distributed data store that can guarantee all three simultaneously.

Proof sketch: Suppose a system is consistent and available; in case of partition, nodes in one side cannot communicate with the other side; to be available, each side must respond to requests; but to maintain consistency, they must coordinate; impossible without communication; thus must sacrifice one.

We can also provide a simple scenario: two nodes A and B separated by partition; client writes to A; reads from B; cannot guarantee both.

We can also mention that CAP is about strong consistency; eventual consistency is a weaker form.

We can also talk about the difference between "strong consistency" and "linearizability".

We can also discuss that many NoSQL databases are AP but can be configured to be CP.
